what_its_for: Potassium is a mineral that your body needs to keep your heart, muscles, and nerves working properly. It is used to treat or prevent low potassium levels in your blood (called hypokalemia). Your doctor may prescribe it if you take certain water pills (diuretics), have poor nutrition, or lose too much potassium due to vomiting or diarrhea.
how_to_take: Take potassium exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow extended-release tablets or capsules whole — do not crush, chew, or break them unless your doctor or pharmacist says it is okay. Take potassium with a full glass of water (at least 8 ounces) and with food or right after a meal to help prevent an upset stomach. If you are using a liquid or powder form, mix it completely in water or juice and drink it slowly over 5 to 10 minutes.
dosing: Your dose will depend on your potassium blood levels and your medical condition. A common adult dose ranges from 20 to 100 mEq (milliequivalents) per day, taken in divided doses. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not take more or less than prescribed. Your doctor will likely check your blood levels regularly to adjust your dose as needed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one, as this can cause dangerously high potassium levels.
storage: Store potassium at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct light, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medication down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about safe disposal options or a local drug take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking salt substitutes or other potassium supplements unless your doctor approves, as these can raise your potassium levels too high. Limit or avoid foods extremely high in potassium (such as large amounts of bananas, oranges, and tomatoes) unless your doctor tells you otherwise. Avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) or naproxen without checking with your doctor, as they can affect potassium levels. Do not stop taking potassium suddenly without talking to your doctor.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: irregular or slow heartbeat, muscle weakness or paralysis, numbness or tingling in your hands or feet, severe stomach pain, nausea, or vomiting, difficulty breathing, feeling faint or lightheaded, or black or tarry stools (which may mean stomach bleeding). These could be signs of potassium levels that are too high or too low, or a serious reaction.
when_it_works: Your potassium levels may begin to improve within a few days of starting treatment. However, you may not feel any different because low potassium often causes no obvious symptoms. Your doctor will use blood tests to check whether your levels are back to normal. Continue taking potassium for as long as your doctor prescribes, even if you feel fine.
special_populations: Older adults may be more sensitive to potassium and should be monitored closely for high potassium levels. People with kidney problems should use potassium with great caution, as their kidneys may not remove excess potassium well — this can be life-threatening. Pregnant or breastfeeding women should consult their doctor before taking potassium supplements. Children's doses are based on weight and must be determined by a doctor. People taking ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or potassium-sparing diuretics (like spironolactone) need extra monitoring, as these medications can cause potassium levels to rise too high.
